citation.title: The Alternative Annotator Test for LLM-as-a-Judge: How to Statistically Justify Replacing Human Annotators with LLMs
citation.venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 16051-16081, July 27 - August 1, 2025

question: How can researchers show statistically, with a small set of human-annotated examples, that a language model can replace human annotators? The paper proposes the alternative annotator test (alt-test).
data: Ten existing annotated datasets (WAX, LGBTeen, MT-Bench, Framing, CEBaB-A, SummEval, 10K Prompts, CEBaB-S, Lesion, KiloGram) with 3 to 13 annotators each, covering classification, rating, pairwise preference and free-text tasks. Six LLMs (Gemini-1.5 Flash and Pro, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3) and four prompting techniques (zero-shot, few-shot with four demonstrations, chain-of-thought, ensemble). Annotator type and counts are in Table 1 (page 6).
method: Leave-one-out comparison. Each human annotator is excluded in turn, and the LLM is compared with that annotator on how well each aligns with the remaining annotators, instance by instance. A one-sided paired t-test (Wilcoxon signed-rank when fewer than 30 instances) tests whether the LLM is at least as good as the excluded annotator, within a cost-benefit margin epsilon. The p-values across annotators are corrected with the Benjamini-Yekutieli procedure (FDR 0.05). The winning rate omega is the share of annotators the LLM beats; the LLM passes if omega is at least 0.5. The Average Advantage Probability (rho) is used to compare LLMs.

definitions.definition: The true or ground-truth annotations, usually set by expert consensus or heavy quality control. The paper assumes they are unavailable.
definitions.quote: represent the “true” or ground truth annotations and are typically determined through rigorous processes, such as consensus among experts or extensive quality control.

definitions.definition: Share of human annotators that the LLM matches or beats in the test. If at least 0.5 the LLM is taken to be able to replace humans.
definitions.quote: If ω ≥0.5,5 then the LLM wins the majority of human annotators, hence we assert that it can replace human annotators.

definitions.definition: Probability that the LLM annotation is as good as or better than that of a randomly chosen human annotator.
definitions.quote: directly represents the probability that the LLM annotations are as good as or better than those of a randomly chosen annotator.

definitions.definition: An LLM with an advantage probability of 1.
definitions.quote: We define it as an LLM that achieves an advantage probability of ρ = 1

definitions.definition: How much worse than a human the LLM may be and still count as an acceptable replacement. Set by the researcher according to annotator type.
definitions.quote: any value can be valid if the researcher reasonably justifies their choice.

proxies.concept: an LLM can replace human annotators
proxies.indicator: Passing the alt-test: winning rate omega of at least 0.5 after Benjamini-Yekutieli correction at FDR 0.05.
proxies.quote: If ω ≥0.5,5 then the LLM wins the majority of human annotators, hence we assert that it can replace human annotators.

proxies.concept: acceptable loss relative to a human (epsilon)
proxies.indicator: Type of annotator: experts 0.2, skilled annotators 0.15, crowd-workers 0.1.
proxies.quote: For each dataset, we selected ε values based on the type of annotators (as indicated in Table 1): experts (ε = 0.2), skilled annotators (ε = 0.15), and crowd-workers (ε = 0.1).

proxies.indicator: Collective responses of several human annotators, since gold labels are not available.
proxies.quote: a common approach is to approximate them using the collective responses of multiple annotators.

proxies.concept: enough instances for the test to be valid
proxies.indicator: At least 30 annotated instances, the point at which the t-test normality assumption is taken to hold.
proxies.quote: When n < 30, the normality assumption may not hold, and a non-parametric test (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank) should be used.

findings.claim: On nine of the ten datasets at least one LLM, with some prompting technique, passed the alt-test.
findings.quote: on nine datasets, at least one LLM, with some prompting technique, success-fully passed the alt-test

findings.claim: With epsilon 0.2, the LLM usually starts to pass before 100 instances, and in half of the cases before 50.
findings.quote: for ε = 0.2, in most cases, the LLM begins to pass the test before annotating 100 instances, and in half even before 50 instances.

findings.claim: With the stricter epsilon 0.1 (crowd-workers), the test needs about twice as many instances.
findings.quote: With ε = 0.1 the alt-test requires more instances, typically double the amount needed for ε = 0.2, between 100 and 150.

findings.claim: Chain-of-thought prompting made results worse in a large share of cases.
findings.quote: the CoT methodology led to a decline in performance in many cases (45%).

findings.claim: The winning rate depends strongly on how many instances are annotated.
findings.quote: the winning rate ω strongly depends on the number of instances

recommendations.claim: Authors recommend three or more annotators and 50 to 100 instances, depending on task complexity.
recommendations.quote: researchers can recruit a small group of annotators (at least three) to annotate a subset of 50 to 100 examples, depending on the complexity of the task.

recommendations.claim: Authors recommend at least 30 instances for the t-test to be valid.
recommendations.quote: you should have at least 30 instances.

recommendations.claim: Authors recommend epsilon 0.2 for trusted experts and 0.15 for skilled annotators.
recommendations.quote: As a rule of thumb, we recommend setting ε to 0.2 when the annotators are trusted experts and 0.15 when they are skilled annotators

recommendations.claim: Authors recommend expert annotators where possible, and at least highly trained crowd-workers.
recommendations.quote: we recommend using expert annotators whenever possible and, at the very least, highly trained crowd-workers.

recommendations.claim: Authors recommend testing each aspect or domain separately while controlling the false discovery rate across all tests.
recommendations.quote: evaluate it in each setting independently while also controlling for the overall False Discovery Rate (FDR).

recommendations.claim: Authors say stricter thresholds can be used when stakes are high.
recommendations.quote: Stricter thresholds can be used in high-stakes domains.

limitations.point: If human annotators disagree strongly, the LLM is unlikely to pass the test.
limitations.quote: In such cases, it is unlikely that the LLM-as-a-judge will succeed in passing our test.

limitations.point: The test cannot stop misuse, for example with weak human annotators or a single expert.
limitations.quote: our procedure cannot fully prevent such misuse.

limitations.point: The benchmark datasets may overlap with the LLMs' training data.
limitations.quote: datasets used in our experiments may overlap with the training data of the evaluated LLMs.

limitations.point: With only three annotators the winning rate can take only four values, so the 0.5 threshold is coarse.
limitations.quote: with only three annotators, ω value is limited to 0, 1⁄3, 2⁄3, 1.

limitations.point: With two annotators the procedure has no consensus signal.
limitations.quote: the procedure simply checks whether the LLM aligns more with one annotator than the other, lacking a consensus signal.

limitations.point: With strongly imbalanced labels an LLM that always predicts the common label can pass the test through ties.
limitations.quote: an LLM that consistently predicts ‘5’ would succeed and pass our test due to the high proportion of ties

limitations.point: The extracted text has garbled tables and equations, so table values were not quoted or used. Prompts in Appendix G are the paper's own LLM prompts, not instructions to the reader. No instructions addressed to a reader or an AI were found.
